analysis.one_liner: Raises car fuel-efficiency standards about 4% per year and expands tax credits for hybrid and electric vehicles.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan bill never got a vote: introduced in March 2007 with six cosponsors from both parties, it sat in the Senate Finance Committee for the rest of the two-year Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required automakers' whole fleets to reach 27.5 miles per gallon by 2013 and then improve about 4% every year, closing loopholes that had let many trucks and off-road-capable vehicles escape the standards. It also let automakers trade compliance credits with each other and expanded tax credits for hybrid vehicles and for factories building advanced-technology cars and parts. Sponsors argued this would cut oil imports and save drivers money at the pump, while helping US plants retool to build efficient cars.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers, who would spend less on gasoline as fleets became more efficient; the bill's own findings cite $600,000 per minute flowing abroad for oil at $75-a-barrel prices [S3]. The bill also aimed tax credits at domestic automakers and parts makers — its findings cite a University of Michigan study projecting nearly 60,000 domestic jobs from $1.5 billion in clean-car tax incentives [S3] — and buyers of hybrid and lean-burn vehicles, whose credits would no longer be capped by a per-manufacturer limit and would run through 2011 [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Sets a fleet-wide average of 27.5 mpg for all automobiles by model year 2013, with a further 4% increase each year after that, and applies the standards to all automobiles up to 10,000 pounds, ending exclusions for certain light trucks and off-highway-capable vehicles [S2] [S3].
Adds a per-manufacturer floor at 92% of the projected fleet-wide average, so no company could free-ride on other makers' efficiency gains [S3].

Removes the cap on hybrid and advanced lean-burn vehicle tax credits, extends the hybrid credit through 2011, and creates a 35% credit for investments in US factories, engineering, R&D, and worker retraining for advanced-technology vehicles [S2] [S3].
Lets manufacturers sell fuel-economy credits to each other and use multi-year compliance windows of up to four model years, giving the industry flexibility in how it meets the targets [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Automakers would bear the cost of meeting rising standards — the bill's findings note projections that sustained high gas prices would shrink the Detroit Three's profits by $7 billion and put nearly 300,000 US jobs at risk if they failed to adapt [S3]. Taxpayers would fund the expanded vehicle-credit and new 35% manufacturing-credit provisions, some of which could be carried back or forward across 35 tax years [S3]. Part of the compliance cost would likely reach buyers through new-vehicle prices.

drawbacks.text: The bill included escape valves: the Transportation Secretary could set lower standards on 'clear and convincing evidence' that targets were technologically unachievable, unsafe, or not cost effective, and manufacturers could trade credits to cover shortfalls — tools that could let actual fuel savings fall well short of the headline numbers [S3].

Higher standards would impose real compliance costs on automakers, and the new manufacturing and consumer credits would cost the Treasury revenue; the bill's own findings acknowledge the Detroit Three stood to lose $7 billion in profits under sustained high gas prices if they could not adapt [S3].

The 27.5 mpg 2013 target was roughly where the passenger-car standard already stood, so the bill's near-term bite came mainly from the yearly 4% escalator and the broadened vehicle definitions — meaningful, but a slower ramp than some advocates wanted [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For drivers and anyone worried about oil dependence, the gains are large and long-running: lower gasoline bills, reduced imports, and a retooled domestic industry. The costs — compliance spending by automakers, foregone tax revenue, and possibly somewhat higher new-vehicle prices — are real but modest next to the fuel savings, and the bill's credit-trading and compliance flexibilities cushion the transition. Its main design weakness is the set of cost-effectiveness and safety waivers, which gave future administrations room to slow-walk the standards.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee in March 2007, and the committee never acted on it, so it died quietly when the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Sen. Barack Obama introduced the Fuel Economy Reform Act on March 6, 2007, joined by six cosponsors split across both parties — four Republicans (Lugar, Smith, Coleman, Specter) and two Democrats (Biden, Bingaman) [S3] [S4] [S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; that referral was the last entry in its action history for the entire two-year Congress [S5].
The Finance Committee never held a markup or sent the bill to the floor, and no version of it ever received a vote in either chamber before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers and oil companies were better off: no binding yearly efficiency mandates or expanded manufacturing credits took effect through this bill, while drivers went on bearing the cost of imported oil. (Fuel-economy standards were later raised through other legislation in 2007, outside this bill.)

for.name: Sen. Barack Obama
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the floor.

for.name: Sens. Joseph Biden, Gordon Smith, Jeff Bingaman, Norm Coleman, and Arlen Specter
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors, giving the bill bipartisan backing from the start.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance (chaired by Sen. Max Baucus)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after the March 2007 referral — no hearing, markup, or floor report in the two years that followed.

against.name: US and foreign automakers
against.what_they_did: Opposed mandatory yearly fuel-economy increases during the 2007 fuel-economy debate, pressing Congress to keep standards voluntary or flexible.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's support was bipartisan from the start — a Democratic lead sponsor with four Republican and two Democratic cosponsors — and it failed without a party-line vote ever being taken; it simply never left committee.

industries.note: The bill imposed rising fleet-wide efficiency requirements on every manufacturer, while offsetting that with a 35% investment credit for retooling US plants and expanded consumer credits that would sell more hybrids. The industry's resistance to such standards matters for consumers because weaker standards mean higher gasoline bills at the pump.

Higher fuel economy directly reduces gasoline demand, the source of the industry's sales. The bill's findings framed reduced petroleum use as worth at least 50 cents per gallon saved when judging cost effectiveness [S3].

industries.industry: Advanced-vehicle and component makers (hybrid, electric, battery)
industries.note: The manufacturing credit covered up to 35% of investment in US production of hybrids, electric-drive vehicles, batteries, and other components, and uncapped consumer hybrid credits would have expanded that market [S2] [S3].
